content.overview: A dry-room average can hide local zones. Sensor placement, airflow paths, rack arrangement, door activity and load density should be mapped against product evidence.

vocabulary.definition: Local environmental condition that differs meaningfully from the room average.
Extent to which a sensor location reflects the condition relevant to the material or decision.
Recorded arrangement of lots, racks, positions and process-relevant equipment within a drying space.

sections.title: Sensors observe locations
sections.body: A sensor reports its local condition, not every product position. Placement and shielding should match the question being asked.

sections.title: Airflow and loading create zones
sections.body: Obstructions, rack spacing, supply and return paths, and unequal loading can create repeatable spatial patterns that should be investigated rather than averaged away.

sections.title: Maps connect environment to lots
sections.body: A quality system should preserve which lot occupied which location during the observed trend so deviations and outcomes can be scoped.

workedExamples: A return-air sensor remains stable while a sheltered rack dries slowly; the sensor is not wrong, but it is insufficient for that product question.
commonMistakes: Adding sensors without defining decisions they support.
Moving lots without updating the map.
Assuming airflow visualization replaces product measurement.
content.practicalApplication: Build a room map with supply, return, doors, sensors, racks, lots and representative product-sampling locations.
content.summary: Environment data becomes useful when sensor locations and product locations are connected through a controlled load map.
